title: implement intersect_rays_1d

atoms.evidence: same R(u)=O+uD form as 0_1_1; here it's reused not introduced
same 2x2 system as 0_1_1 but now batched across (nrays, nsegments); the geometry is load-bearing
einops.repeat(rays, 'nrays p d -> nrays nsegments p d', nsegments=NS) — canonical pair-every-with-every
mat = t.stack([D, L_1 - L_2], dim=-1) — same as 0_1_1 but now over batched (NR, NS, 2) operands
dets = t.linalg.det(mat); is_singular = dets.abs() < 1e-8; mat[is_singular] = t.eye(2); ... & ~is_singular — exercise markdown spells out the trick step-by-step
sol = t.linalg.solve(mat, vec) on (NR, NS, 2, 2) and (NR, NS, 2) — the batched form replacing the try/except of 0_1_1
.any(dim=-1) reduces (nrays, nsegments) bool to (nrays,); markdown explicitly directs use of t.any
help dropdown explicitly notes mat[is_singular] = t.eye(2) relies on (2,2) broadcasting to (N,2,2)
rays = rays[..., :2] / segments = segments[..., :2] discard the z dim via basic indexing; also mat[is_singular] = ... is the assignment form

notes: Densest early exercise: 10 atoms. The 'replace singular with identity' trick is named in the exercise text and is the singular pedagogical climax. unbind-tuple-unpack is not used — the solution uses indexed slicing (rays[:, :, 0], rays[:, :, 1]) instead of unpacking, so I omitted it (seed predicted it). einops-reduce-min not used — exercise reduces with t.any, not einops.reduce.
